note:
WILLIAM

So what does this ask us to build? Integration and rigor, not invention.

Workload identity for every agent: SPIFFE and SPIRE. Reach enforced on that identity: Linkerd, and plain Kubernetes NetworkPolicy. Authorization on every call at the tool boundary: agentgateway. A live autonomy level, per identity: an OpenFeature flag. The agent kept out of its own guardrails: Kyverno, at admission. And Git as the only way to change any of it.

These are the exact projects in the demo you're about to see. Almost all CNCF; agentgateway lives in the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation.

What's new is small: agent identity and limits as declarative objects, and per-tool authorization for agent protocols like MCP. A thin new layer on a deep and stable foundation. Every one of these has a production-grade project behind it today.

Let's start at the core: who is acting.

[verify: agentgateway joined AAIF 2026-06-04 (agentgateway.dev blog)]

Source: William Rizzo, KCD Sofia 2026 keynote, slide 15; Northstar's projects (deploy/platform/)

WILLIAM

The core first: who is acting. Everything after this keys off it. So, one minute on the two projects that answer it, with one picture: a passport.

SPIFFE is the standard: what a passport looks like. An ID for a workload, not a person: spiffe, northstar.local, the namespace, the service account. And the document that carries it, the SVID: short-lived, and signed.

SPIRE is the passport office: it issues them. It runs an agent on every node. When a pod asks for its identity, the agent checks where that pod really runs, its namespace and its service account, and only then does the SPIRE server sign.

Follow the four steps. The pod asks, over a local socket, with no secret. SPIRE checks. SPIRE signs something that expires soon and renews on its own. And the pod shows its passport at the gateway, on every call.

And the agent card the agent publishes? That's the brochure, not the passport. Anyone can print a brochure.

No password to leak, nothing to rotate by hand. The identity is proven by where the workload runs, not by what it claims. Both are CNCF graduated.

Source: deploy/platform/spire/registration.yaml (ClusterSPIFFEID templates, selectors k8s:ns and k8s:sa); the SPIFFE CSI driver socket; spiffe.io docs; SPIFFE and SPIRE graduated in the CNCF in 2022

WILLIAM

Here's the passport office's rule, as config. The ID is built from the pod's namespace and service account. Where it runs. Nothing the agent says goes into it. The gateway reads this passport on every call; you'll see it in Kasper's trace.

Source: deploy/platform/spire/registration.yaml

WILLIAM

Ring 1, reach: what may the agent connect to? Two layers, one for the way in and one for the way out.

The way in is Linkerd, a service mesh: a small proxy beside every pod that checks who is calling, by the caller's mTLS identity. The tool server, payments-mcp, denies everything by default. One authorization policy lets exactly one identity in: the gateway's. The policy decision service is set up the same way. So an agent that tries to go around the gateway, straight to the tool, gets a 403, and Linkerd counts the refusal.

The way out is a plain Kubernetes network policy, enforced in the node. The agents may reach the gateway, for tools and for the model, and nothing on the internet. Not even the model provider: the model sits behind the gateway too. That's the next slide but one.

SAY: "Go around the gateway: 403, and counted."

IF ASKED why two tools: Linkerd's own egress rule applies to a whole namespace and matches only the name the client claims; a network policy holds even for a pod that skips its proxy.

Source: deploy/platform/reach/linkerd-policies.yaml (Server accessPolicy: deny; AuthorizationPolicy payments-mcp-gateway-only, policy-decision-service-gateway-only; MeshTLSAuthentication agentgateway); deploy/platform/reach/network-policies.yaml (settlement-agent-egress, claims-agent-egress: agentgateway on 3000 and 4000, plus DNS, the collector and the Linkerd control plane; no ipBlock)

WILLIAM

agentgateway is the only door to the tools, and, in a moment, to the model. For a tool call, three checks, in order, all in one config file.

One: the passport. No valid SPIFFE token, 401.
Two: one CEL rule. Only two workloads may use the tools at all: the settlement agent, and the reviewer UI when a person releases a payment. Anyone else, even with a valid passport, 403. And execute_payment above fifty thousand euros is refused, always.
Three: everything else goes to the policy service. And if the policy service can't answer, the answer is no: fail closed.

Why two ways to say no? CEL is fast and needs no code, but it can't look anything up, so it holds the facts that never change. The everyday limit depends on who's asking, how much we trust them today, and the ledger. That needs a lookup, so the gateway asks.

Source: deploy/platform/agentgateway/config.yaml (condensed: the route's authorization rule and mcpGuardrails processor)

WILLIAM

The same gateway has a second door: the model. Every model call from both agents goes through it.

Three checks again. The passport: no SPIFFE token, 401. Then one rule: only the claims agent and the settlement agent may call a model at all. Anything else, even with a valid passport, gets a 403. Then a list of models: ask for one that isn't on it, 404, and the request never leaves the cluster.

And the API key lives here, in the gateway, read from a mounted secret. The agents hold none, and the network policy gives them no road to the internet. So the gateway's span says which agent called which model, and what it cost, under the same passport.

SAY: "The agent holds no key. The platform does."

IF ASKED whether the gateway reads the prompt: it can. agentgateway ships prompt guards for model traffic: regex and PII rules, a webhook, and hosted moderation services. None are on in Northstar. The injected claim is flagged afterwards, by AgentEvals.

Source: deploy/platform/agentgateway/config.yaml (the llm block, condensed); measured on the cluster 2026-10-28: no token 401 "no bearer token found", reviewer-ui's valid SVID 403 "authorization failed", an unlisted model 404 model_not_found

WILLIAM

Ring two has a second half: how free is the agent today? That's a live setting, its autonomy level, and it's a feature flag. OpenFeature is the CNCF standard for asking about feature flags. The question is standard; what answers it is pluggable. Think of a wall socket: every appliance fits the same socket, whatever power station is behind it.

On the left, where the level lives. A FeatureFlag, a plain Kubernetes object. flagd, the provider, serves it as a sidecar. And the decision service asks one question through the OpenFeature SDK: what is the autonomy level, for this SPIFFE ID? It takes the caller from the passport on the call.

On the right, the config. The flag gives one value to one identity, the settlement agent's SPIFFE ID. The default is assisted; Kasper's demo sets it to autonomous. Under it, the policy service's table: assisted, zero euros, so a person signs every payout; autonomous, up to six thousand, and above that a person decides. Any other caller has no row, and no row means deny.

Why a flag for a policy knob? It changes without a deploy. The change is a one-word diff you can review. It's answered per caller. And every evaluation leaves a trace: the decision becomes a span with rule, limit, amount, caller and level. If flagd can't answer, the level falls back to assisted.

Same agent, same code, same image. Only the flag decides how free.

Keep one question in your head: if one value on one object decides this much, who may change that value? That's the keystone.

Source: deploy/platform/openfeature/featureflag.yaml (condensed); platform/policy-decision-service/pds/rules.py EXECUTE_LIMITS; pds/autonomy.py

WILLIAM

And the keystone. That flag is one value on one object. So who may change it? If the answer is "the agent", every limit you've seen is a suggestion.

The objects that define the agent's authority: its flag, its permissions, the policies, the gateway routes, its SPIFFE registration. If the agent's own identity tries to change any of them, Kyverno denies it at admission. A person or a pipeline, through a reviewed commit, is applied. The rule itself is a few lines of Kyverno, in CEL: if the request comes from any service account in the agents' namespace, deny.

And it holds even when someone makes a mistake: grant the agent permission by accident, so RBAC says yes, and Kyverno still says no. Kasper ends the demo on exactly that.

The agent acts inside its bounds. It cannot rewrite them.

Source: deploy/platform/kyverno/keystone-policy.yaml; William Rizzo, KCD Sofia 2026, slide 12

WILLIAM, then KASPER

WILLIAM: That's the first word. Decide: the platform, not the agent, says what an agent may do. You've seen the rings that decide it.

But a decision you can't see afterwards is a decision you have to take on trust. The other two words are Kasper's. Kasper?

HANDOVER: Kasper takes the clicker here.

KASPER: Thanks, William. Trace: what the agent actually did. Let's run it, and look.
